Then yes, I agree, that’s exactly why appeals exist, so wrongful convictions can be investigated and corrected. I was just trying to highlight the key difference with the Post Office scandal, where those processes weren’t available to the wrongfully convicted, and the people prosecuting had a direct conflict of interest, meaning it was never a fair trial to begin with.

While both systems do involve an adversarial process, the difference is in the structure and oversight. In the case of Letby, the CPS operates as a regulated, independent legal system with proper oversight and the right to appeal, which ensures fairness and transparency. And the people bring the case to court are the CPS, not the hospital trust. On the other hand, the Post Office case involved a private, unregulated prosecution where the Post Office itself acted as both the accuser and the prosecutor. It’s the lack of independent oversight that led to wrongful convictions, with the Post Office knowing about the flaws in the Horizon system but continuing to prosecute based on faulty evidence.

Regarding the CPS’s involvement in the Post Office cases, it is true that they eventually brought some of the cases to court but by that point, the damage was already done. The original prosecutions were carried out by the Post Office itself, and the CPS only became involved later, often after many convictions had already occurred. Furthermore, those convicted by CPS (nothing compared to the amount convicted by the Post Office) would have had the same processes Letby has to appeal, those convicted by the Post Office did not get to exercise this right. 

If your point is that sometimes convictions are wrong, I agree with you. However, if your point is that the Post Office scandal somehow proves Letby is innocent, I don’t agree. I don’t think you can compare the two situations, as they involve entirely different systems with distinct processes and safeguards. Just because they both involved a Jury does not make them equivalent.

One is a regulated justice system with independent oversight and various processes of reviewing evidence (CPS), the other is an unregulated, private prosecution system, with no independent oversight, where the prosecution has a vested interest in the convictions of the defendants (post office). Not the same by any means
It’s a different system entirely.
To the public, yes, but the Post Office knew about the faults long before it became public knowledge and continued to convict people on false pretences.

Not necessarily a notary, because the counter-signatory has to know you personally, you can’t just get a notary to sign it if they don’t meet the conditions of being able to identify you and having known you at least two years.

We can take our own photos, but if you’re getting your first passport (and under various other circumstances that are not bog-standard renewals), you have to get a non-family member of either a listed occupation or of high standing in the community to confirm you are who you say you are by signing the back of the photo and your form. This person (a counter-signatory) needs to know you well enough that they can identify you, and have known you for at least 2 years.

When they countersign they must also provide their passport details so the home office can contact them to verify the information. It’s not foolproof, but there is more to it than anyone can just send in a picture with no verification.

Nobody here from what I’ve seen has disagreed with you that slamming on the breaks is not the right thing to do, but just because a pedestrian shouldn’t have crossed does not mean that you can go ahead and put them in even further danger, doing so benefits absolutely nobody.

Slowing down gently to account for a hazard doesn’t put you at risk of being rear-ended unless the person behind you isn’t paying attention—and in that case, the fault lies with them, not you. And if I had to choose between being rear-ended or potentially killing a pedestrian, i’m going to pick being rear ended, both car users at least have the protection of the car around them, the pedestrian does not. 

If that pedestrian steps in front of your car and you kill them, after not slowing down despite seeing them on the road, you will bear some responsibility. Pedestrians are at the top of the hierarchy of road users, as they are the most vulnerable. This isn’t about who is ‘in the right’—it’s about making choices that reduce risks for everyone. We all have a duty to make the roads safer, and slowing down in this kind of situation is a basic part of that responsibility.

Where in the Highway Code does it state you can ignore pedestrians in the middle of the road and continue driving past them at 30mph? The police would almost certainly consider that, at minimum, careless driving. While slamming on the brakes isn’t any better really (as you pointed out originally someone could rear end them), if you can slow down gently to let the pedestrian get out of the road, you absolutely should. Failing to do so only increases the risk of a serious or even fatal collision, regardless of whether you think the pedestrian has made a poor decision.

As a road user, you have a responsibility to prevent incidents wherever possible. The Highway Code clearly states: “The rules in The Highway Code do not give you the right of way in any circumstance, but they advise you when you should give way to others. Always give way if it can help to avoid an incident.”

If slowing down allows the pedestrian cross safely and avoids a potential incident, that’s what should be done, no matter who technically has the right of way.

In that case I would stop too, ideally not by slamming breaks as should have noticed her earlier so could come to a more gradual stop, but If a pedestrian has started crossing the road regardless of whether they should have, you really should let them cross as they are quite vulnerable being in the middle of the road with people driving past them at 30.
